title: Causal language and strength of inference in academic and media articles shared in social media (CLAIMS): A systematic review
screen_reason: Despite the 'systematic review' label, this is a PRIMARY content analysis: the authors sampled the 64 most-shared health media articles (and the 50 academic articles behind them) from NewsWhip Facebook/Twitter sharing data for 2015 and had trained reviewers code each one. It reports a share of items judged INACCURATE against an external ground truth (the underlying academic study): 'Fifty-eight percent of media articles were found to have inaccurately reported the question, results, intervention, or population of the academic study.' That is a CONTENT estimate with a denominator (64 media articles). Two headline overstatement measures are also reported and are coded as QUALITY (a wholly true article can be labelled as using 'too strong' causal language).

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language media outlets; most common domains CBS News, The Guardian, The New York Times)
estimates.platform: Media/news articles sampled by Facebook and Twitter shares (NewsWhip Insights)
estimates.date: Media articles published 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2015; NewsWhip queried 3 May 2016; reviews completed August-October 2016
estimates.measure_type: % of most-shared health media articles that inaccurately reported the question, results, intervention or population of the academic study they covered
estimates.denominator: 64 unique media articles (covering 50 academic articles) accepted for review, drawn in descending share order from the 1,418 non-duplicate most-shared 2015 health news URLs on Facebook and Twitter
estimates.definition: An article counted in the numerator if the arbitrating reviewer judged that it did not accurately describe the question, results, intervention or population of the academic study it reported on, checked directly against that academic article
estimates.misinfo_def: “The pathway from evidence generation to consumption contains many steps which can lead to overstatement or misinformation”; operationally, media articles that “inaccurately reported the question, results, intervention, or population of the academic study”
estimates.source_quote: Fifty-eight percent of media articles were found to have inaccurately reported the question, results, intervention, or population of the academic study.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results section (p. 2); the figure is not repeated with a raw count in the body
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pool of 21 reviewers, all holding at least a master's degree and 19/21 holding or pursuing a doctorate in a health/quantitative field; each article read by two randomly assigned independent reviewers plus one arbitrating reviewer who produced the final rating, using a purpose-built review tool. Ground truth = the academic article itself. Reliability reported only for the causal-inference and causal-language scales (primary reviewers within one category in 96% of cases, exact agreement 58%; causal language 93% within one category, 47% exact); NO agreement statistic is reported for the accuracy measure specifically.
estimates.moderator_quote: In the media article assessment, reviewers assessed whether the media article accurately described the same relationship as the scientific article and the strength of causal language used, using the same research question as in the scientific article.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator: this figure is reported ONLY in the structured abstract, with no raw count in the Results body (58% of 64 would be ~37 articles). breadth coded 'false' because the coding is a direct accuracy judgement of what the article said about the study, not a spin/tone judgement; an adjudicator could defensibly code 'misleading' since the label bundles mis-description of the population/intervention with mis-description of the results. denom_selection=curated because the sample is rank-truncated to the most-shared articles and is explicitly NOT representative of media output ('this sample is unlikely to be representative of the broader work in both academia and media').

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language media outlets; most common domains CBS News, The Guardian, The New York Times)
estimates.platform: Media/news articles sampled by Facebook and Twitter shares (NewsWhip Insights)
estimates.date: Media articles published 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2015
estimates.measure_type: % of most-shared health media articles written using causal language judged too strong given the language used in the academic study
estimates.denominator: 64 unique media articles accepted for review
estimates.definition: An article counted if the arbitrating reviewer directly indicated its causal language was 'too strong' given the language used in the academic study
estimates.misinfo_def: “issues with systematic selection, spin, overstatement, inaccuracy, and weak evidence are likely to accumulate by the time scientific research reaches the consumer”
estimates.source_quote: 48% (n = 31) of media articles were written using causal language that was too strong given the language used in the academic study
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 21-reviewer pool, two independent reviewers plus an arbitrator; language rated on a 3-point Weak/Moderate/Strong scale plus a too weak / accurately descriptive / too strong judgement. 93% of primary reviewer pairs chose within one category of each other for causal language, 47% exact matches (reported for the academic-article rating).
estimates.moderator_quote: For both academic and media articles, reviewers were asked whether they believed the strength of causal language was too weak, accurately descriptive, or too strong given the strength of causal inference.
estimates.notes: Coded QUALITY, not CONTENT: 'causal language too strong' is a spin/overstatement judgement, and a wholly accurate article reporting a true association can receive the label. Excluded from prevalence. borderline=true flags that a reader could easily mistake this for a misinformation share. QUOTE NOTE: the quote is trimmed to the span that is contiguous in the extracted .txt; the sentence continues '..., which were themselves rated as being overstated on average given the strength of causal inference.' but the final word falls after a page/figure break in the text file.

estimates.country: Not stated (academic articles in international peer-reviewed journals)
estimates.platform: Peer-reviewed academic articles sampled via Facebook/Twitter shares of media coverage
estimates.date: Academic articles covered by 2015 media articles
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-shared health academic studies that used causal language too strong for their assessed strength of causal inference
estimates.definition: A study counted if the arbitrating reviewer directly indicated the study used causal language too strong for the independently assessed strength of causal inference
estimates.misinfo_def: “issues with systematic selection, spin, overstatement, inaccuracy, and weak evidence are likely to accumulate by the time scientific research reaches the consumer”
estimates.source_quote: Reviewers directly indicated that 34% (n = 17) of academic studies used causal language which was too strong for the assessed causal inference.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 21-reviewer pool with two independent reviews plus arbitration; strength of causal inference rated on a 5-point scale, causal language on a 3-point scale. Primary reviewers within one category in 96% of cases for strength of inference, exact agreement 58%.
estimates.moderator_quote: The final assessment of this section summarizes the reviewer's overall evaluation for the strength of causal inference on the same 5-point scale (Very low, Low, Moderate, High, Very high strength) with detailed prompts on which to base a decision.
estimates.notes: QUALITY for the same reason as the media-article overstatement row: overstated causal language is not a truth/falsity judgement. Excluded from prevalence.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons. 1) 'Seventy percent of academic studies were considered low or very low strength of inference, with only 6% considered high or very high' (abstract) — a risk-of-bias rating of the underlying research, i.e. QUALITY of evidence rather than accuracy of communicated content; it is also a cross-category sum in the body (54% Low + 16% Very low), so I left it out under R4 (quality over quantity) rather than adding a third near-duplicate QUALITY row. 2) The Fig-3 cross-check figures — '42% (n = 21) of academic studies and 67% (n = 43) of media articles were found to have language which was stronger than the causal inference' — are a SECOND operationalisation of the same overstatement construct (derived from the theoretical-region definition rather than the reviewers' direct judgement); they would be definition_variant rows of the 34%/48% rows and are omitted to avoid double-counting. 3) '83% (n = 38) of the 46 media articles linked to Low/Very-low-inference studies were written about using moderate or strong causal language' and '45% (n = 16) of the 35 Low/Very-low academic articles were written with strong or moderate causal language' are conditional subgroup versions of the same measure. 4) '55% (n = 35) of media articles had causal language stronger than the academic article', '39% (n = 25) matched', '6% (n = 4) weaker' — the same three-category language-comparison distribution. 5) '68% (938,596/1,375,152) of Facebook shares and 45% (189,777/423,996) of Twitter shares' describe the share coverage of the SCREENED sample, not a misinformation share, and are not a CONCENTRATION row in the review's sense (they are cumulative shares of a screened rank range, not a top-X%-of-users/sources statement with both a group percentage and an activity percentage), so R1 cannot be satisfied. 6) Study-design descriptives (14% RCTs, 54% prospective cohorts, etc.) are irrelevant.

rob.design: Purposive rank-truncated content analysis with PRISMA/PROSPERO registration (CRD42016045197). Frame: NewsWhip Insights crawler, keyword query for 2015 health news reporting on research; 11,349 unique URLs, top 1,000 per platform merged to 1,418 non-duplicate links; screened in descending share order until 50 academic articles were reached, which occurred at the 231st media article, yielding 64 media articles. Coding: 21 reviewers (19/21 doctoral), two independent primary reviewers plus one arbitrator per article, blinded to each other's identity, recusal allowed; results from arbitrator reviews only. Reliability: primary reviewers within one category in 96% of cases on strength of inference (58% exact), 93% within one category on causal language (47% exact); no agreement statistic for the accuracy measure. Explicit non-representativeness caveat by the authors.
rob.item6_quote: In the media article assessment, reviewers assessed whether the media article accurately described the same relationship as the scientific article and the strength of causal language used, using the same research question as in the scientific article.
rob.item10_quote: In total, reviewers identified 50 review sets, consisting of 50 academic articles with 64 unique media articles associated with them (S2 Fig, S2 and S3 Tables).
